c2_berit_note.title: A note in the book
c2_berit_note.text: Between two pages of the old book there is a note in thin brown ink: “Rest the field. Rest yourself. — B.” You read it twice. Then you look at your hands.

c2_k_rest.text: The note in the book flutters in the wind. It says what it always says.

pages.text: Every Landing Day, old Jan shouts “HERE!” for Moonedge, so the name will not get lonely. No letter ever came. Today one has.
Mei, the barge captain, walks the letter up the muddy hill herself, which captains do not do. Old Jan comes puffing behind. “Wanted to be there,” he wheezes. “The first time it counted.”

The writing is round and quick: your mother's. “Come home when you are ready, my love. The house is small, but the table is long. Your cousin asks after you.” A pressed hazel leaf falls out of the fold and lands on your boot.

c2_walls.title: Crooked walls
c2_walls.text: The walls of the cottage stand. You built them alone, and it shows. One leans a little to the left. You step back, look at them for a long time, and decide that they are perfect.

pages.text: A boy waits at your gate with a basket of herbs bigger than his arms. “You're the Moonedge one,” he says. “You used to carry a bucket bigger than you.” You did.
“Why is that wall crooked? Does it hurt when you hammer? Did you know sage is good for a cough?” He asks too many questions. You find, to your surprise, that you do not mind.

c2_stumps.title: Too many stumps
c2_stumps.text: So many stumps, for such a small farm. Their tops are clean and flat. Someone cut the forest back, long ago, and nobody planted anything in its place.

c2_lark.title: A visitor on the new road

pages.text: A man is sitting on one of your crates. You did not hear him come. “You,” you say. “Me,” says Lark, as if that were lovely for both of you. “Marvellous road. You put stones in a row, and then people can find you.”

He stacks a crate on yours, crooked. “It's crooked,” you say. “It's standing,” says Lark. He reads your list off the fence in a stern voice. “Roof. Before frost. No please.” He turns it over. “It's signed. It's signed you.”

“A woman once built a lighthouse,” says Lark. “She was so busy making it better that she never went out to see it shine.” Then the crate is empty. On your list you cross out “frost” and write “soon”. The crooked crate stays crooked.
You clear the last black beam from the barn. Then you stop. The burn does not start at the roof, where lightning would strike. It starts low, in the corner where the hay was kept.
You sit back on your heels. Lightning does not start low. You look at that corner for a long time, and your hands go cold. Then you pick up the beam and carry it out. Not yet.

c2_compost.title: A tidy pit
c2_compost.text: Behind the old barn is a compost pit, lined with flat stones, its corners squared by somebody who cared very much. It is clean, dry and empty. Somebody sold every straw. On the lid, scratched: “Feed the ground and it feeds you. — B.”

c2_cottage.title: A roof of your own
c2_cottage.text: The roof is on, and it does not leak. You sit under it while the first rain taps on the thatch. Then you take a sheet of paper and write home: “I'm staying a bit longer.” Your hand shakes only a little.

pages.text: Something very slow is crossing the yard: a tortoise, like a stone that has decided to travel. She goes right past the little house you built for her. She walks all the way to the pond, and sits on the flat, mossy stone.

That is where the spring used to rise. You know it at once. You have a great deal to do, and you sit down beside her anyway. The pond fills a little. And the old rhyme comes back: “Slow shell keeps the water clean.”

c2_hook.title: A blackened hook
c2_hook.text: You find the old iron hook in the ash, made to hold a lantern. You hang it on the new doorpost. Old Jan sees it and stops grumbling. “Never past the sill. Berit's rule.” “Then how did the fire get in?” Jan coughs.

pages.text: Back in the room, somebody has fallen asleep on the floor with their mouth open. “Did you find out who started it?” asks Minena. “The fire?” “Not then,” you say. “I didn't want to.” “Why not?” You do not answer that.
“And the man on the fence? With the buttons. Was he funny?” “Very.” “Was that good?” “It made him hard to talk to,” you say. Nobody understands what you mean. That is all right.

c2_k_bunny_carrots.text: The bunny sits beside the carrots, very still, looking at the sky. As if carrots were something she had never heard of.

c2_k_tortoise_yard.text: The tortoise has been crossing the yard all morning. She is nearly in the middle. She looks very pleased about it.

c2_k_hen_cow.text: A hen walks right under the cow. The cow looks down. The hen looks up. Neither of them will move first.
